name: Circuit Hymns for a Closing Year
description:
Recorded over eleven months in 2199 and released on the first day of 2200 — a date chosen deliberately, as the city's corporate media was consumed with Millennium-adjacent spectacle and unlikely to pay attention — Circuit Hymns for a Closing Year is a collaborative album by a rotating collective of Circuit-tier musicians organized by Adaeze Holm-Nkemdirim, a veteran folk singer and community organizer from the eastern Circuit who had been running informal recording sessions in her apartment for years. The album features thirty-one contributors across sixteen tracks, ranging from teenage apprentices at the Meridian fabrication yards to retired logistics workers in their seventies. The music is rooted in what the liner notes call 'the actual sound of where we live': work songs built on Yoruba rhythmic patterns, lullabies that blend Finnish runic singing with Brazilian embolada vocal technique, drinking songs with lyrical structures borrowed from Mongolian urtiin duu, and quiet hymns that belong to no tradition anyone can name precisely.

Standout tracks include 'The Shift Ends at Five' — a seven-voice round about the specific joy of a work day ending that became a ubiquitous Circuit anthem — 'Meridian, My Meridian' (a sardonic love song to the city that manages to be genuinely tender), and 'What the Chrome Costs,' a duet between Holm-Nkemdirim and a then-unknown seventeen-year-old vocalist named Sani Ekwueme-Borg that stops most listeners cold. The album was self-released on data chip at Φ5 per copy, with free copies distributed to community centers. It has never been on any official feed.
creator: Adaeze Holm-Nkemdirim and the Circuit Hymns Collective
genre: Circuit folk / communal work song / polyrhythmic hymn
audience: Circuit workers and families, community organizers, Shelf listeners who obtain chip copies through community centers, folk music archivists, anyone who has ever worked a long shift
cultural_impact: Circuit Hymns for a Closing Year is the most widely owned self-released album in Meridian 88's history by estimated chip count — over 40,000 copies in circulation by 2215, with no official distribution and no corporate involvement. 'The Shift Ends at Five' is sung in Circuit pubs, at labor rallies, and reportedly at a Tier 3 teacher's retirement party that a Vantablack Media executive attended by accident. Adaeze Holm-Nkemdirim has refused every label offer since the album's release. Sani Ekwueme-Borg, the seventeen-year-old on 'What the Chrome Costs,' went on to become one of the most celebrated voices of the 2210s, and has repeatedly said in interviews that the album 'taught me what music is for.'
known_fans: Shelf families who received free copies
Sani Ekwueme-Borg fans who trace backward to the source
story_hooks: Adaeze Holm-Nkemdirim has gone missing; the Circuit Hymns Collective is quietly looking for her without going to corporate security, and the last thing she told a friend was that someone had offered her something for the master recordings that she was afraid to refuse and afraid to accept.

A data chip copy of Circuit Hymns surfaces in a Tier 5 estate auction, listed as a 'historical artifact' with a reserve price of Φ3,000 — and the Circuit community is furious in a way that might become something more than furious.
The thirty-one contributors to the album are being contacted one by one by an entity claiming to represent 'archival preservation interests'; most are confused; two have stopped responding to anyone.
